topics.name: The nature of God and religious language

cards: Prisoners see only shadows (the world of appearances); the escaped prisoner sees the sun (the Form of the Good). The philosopher should return to educate others.
Perfect, unchanging Forms exist in a separate realm and are known through reason; the physical world contains imperfect copies.
Material, efficient, formal and final causes. The final cause is the purpose (telos) of something.
An unmoved mover that causes motion by attraction as a final cause; eternal, immaterial and perfect.
Plato trusted reason over the senses (rationalism); Aristotle trusted empirical observation (empiricism).
The highest Form, which illuminates all others, as the sun lets us see objects in the cave analogy.
Aristotle's third man argument; the Forms can't be proved; is there a Form of mud or hair?
The final cause may be a human projection; science explains things without purpose (Darwin, Dawkins).
The soul is immortal and belongs to the world of Forms; the body is a prison. Tripartite soul: reason, spirit and appetite.
The soul is the form of the body, not separate from it; it cannot survive death.
The mind (thinking substance) is distinct from the body (extended substance): 'I think, therefore I am'.
Gilbert Ryle called dualism a 'category mistake' and 'the ghost in the machine'. Dawkins: humans are 'survival machines' for genes.
The charioteer (reason) controls two horses: spirit (noble) and appetite (unruly).
Like the impression in wax, the soul is inseparable from the body.
How can a non-physical mind affect a physical body? Descartes suggested the pineal gland.
Mental states are identical to brain states; criticised by qualia (what it is like to experience).
Includes arguments from motion, causation, contingency and design (the fifth way: the arrow and archer analogy).
The complexity and purpose of a watch imply a designer; similarly, the universe and the eye imply God.
The analogy is weak; the universe could have come from chance (Epicurean hypothesis); the designer could be many gods or imperfect.
Everything has a cause, so there must be an uncaused first cause (God). Kalam version: the universe began to exist.
Natural selection explains apparent design without a designer.
Hume: we can't infer causes beyond experience. Russell: the universe is 'just there, and that's all'. Possible infinite regress.
Teleological arguments start from order and purpose; cosmological arguments start from existence and causation.
Contingency: everything that exists depends on something else, so there must be a necessary being.
Copleston argued from contingency for a necessary being; Russell rejected the need for an explanation of the universe.
Tennant: the universe is fine-tuned for life, suggesting design.
God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; existing in reality is greater than existing only in the mind, so God must exist.
Anselm's logic would prove the existence of a perfect island, which is absurd.
Existence is not a predicate: it adds nothing to the concept of a thing.
God is a supremely perfect being; existence is a perfection, so God exists, just as a triangle must have three angles.
Ontological arguments are a priori (reason alone); design and cosmological arguments are a posteriori (experience).
God's existence is necessary; a being that cannot not exist is greater than one that can.
The argument only applies to God, a necessary being, not to contingent things like islands.
Visions, numinous experiences (Otto: mysterium tremendum et fascinans), mystical experiences, conversion and corporate experiences (e.g. the Toronto Blessing).
Mystical experiences are ineffable, noetic, transient and passive; judged by their fruits.
Principle of credulity (trust experiences unless there's reason not to) and principle of testimony (trust what others report).
Explained by psychology (Freud: wish fulfilment), physiology (temporal lobe) or drugs; experiences are subjective and unverifiable.
Shared experiences, e.g. the Toronto Blessing (1994) with laughter and falling; criticised as mass hysteria.
A change of belief or way of life, e.g. St Paul on the road to Damascus.
A feeling of awe and wonder before the holy, a 'wholly other' presence.
May be self-authenticating for the believer, but less convincing as proof for others.
Mackie: God is omnipotent and wholly good, yet evil exists; this is inconsistent.
Rowe: the amount of pointless suffering (e.g. a fawn dying in a forest fire) makes God's existence unlikely.
Evil is a privation of good; it came from the free will of angels and humans (the Fall); natural evil is a punishment. Soul-deciding.
Humans are created in the image of God and must grow into his likeness through a 'vale of soul-making'; epistemic distance allows free choice.
Augustine conflicts with evolution and is unjust to later generations; Hick's view struggles with the scale of suffering (e.g. the Holocaust) and universal salvation.
Moral evil is caused by human choices; natural evil comes from the natural world (earthquakes, disease).
God allows evil because a world with free agents is better than one with robots.
Hick: God keeps a distance so humans can freely choose to love him.
Ivan Karamazov rejects any heaven built on the suffering of innocent children.
God can do anything logically possible (Aquinas) or can do anything at all (Descartes).
Boethius: God is timeless and sees all of time at once. Swinburne: God is everlasting and moves through time.
If God knows our future actions, are we free? Boethius: God sees our actions as an eternal present, so foreknowledge doesn't cause them.
Apophatic: the via negativa describes God by what he is not (Pseudo-Dionysius). Cataphatic: positive statements through analogy and symbol.
Aquinas: analogy of attribution and proportion allow meaningful talk about God.
Religious language points to and participates in what it symbolises: God is the 'ground of being'.
Ayer's verification principle: statements are meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable; religious statements are meaningless.
Flew: religious claims die 'the death of a thousand qualifications'. Hare's bliks and Mitchell's partisan respond.
Meaning comes from use within a form of life; religious language is meaningful to believers.
God is perfectly good; questioned by the problem of evil and divine commands in scripture.
Is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?
Can God create a stone he cannot lift? A challenge to the coherence of omnipotence.
Saying only what God is not may leave nothing meaningful to believe in.
A non-falsifiable way of seeing the world, like the student convinced all dons want to kill him.
Faith in the stranger despite ambiguous evidence; believers allow evidence to count against belief but not decisively.
Humans have a God-given telos; reason discovers primary precepts: preserve life, reproduce, educate, live in society, worship God.
Specific rules derived from the primary precepts, e.g. no abortion follows from preserving life.
An action with a good and a bad effect is permissible if the act is good, the bad effect isn't intended, it is not the means to the good, and there is proportionate reason.
Assumes a single human nature; the naturalistic fallacy; inflexible in complex situations.
Eternal law, divine law, natural law and human law.
Humans may pursue apparent goods by mistake, but reason helps identify real goods.
Aquinas: both the intention and the act must be good.
Universal, based on reason, gives clear rules and is accessible to non-religious people.
The only intrinsic good is agape (selfless love); act in the most loving way in each situation.
Love is the only good; love is the ruling norm; love and justice are the same; love wills the neighbour's good; only the end justifies the means; love decides there and then.
Hard to predict consequences; too individualistic; agape is subjective; William Temple supported it, but the Pope condemned it in 1952.
Legalism (rigid rules), antinomianism (no rules) and situationism (love guides each case).
Jesus' command to love your neighbour and the Good Samaritan underpin situation ethics.
Mrs Bergmeier, who became pregnant to be released from a prison camp to her family.
Flexible, person-centred and based on Christian love.
Kant: the only thing good without qualification is a good will acting from duty.
Hypothetical: if you want X, do Y. Categorical: unconditional moral commands.
Universal law (act only on maxims you can will to be universal), persons as ends (never only as means) and the kingdom of ends.
Freedom, immortality and God are assumed for morality to make sense (the summum bonum).
Conflicts of duties; ignores consequences (the murderer at the door); too rigid; ignores emotions.
The motive, not the consequences, determines moral worth: acting from duty, not merely in accordance with it.
A shopkeeper who is honest for profit acts in accordance with duty but not from duty.
Kant: moral agents give themselves the moral law through reason, rather than following authority.
Universal, respects human dignity and gives clear rules that don't depend on predicting outcomes.
The right act produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number; measured with the hedonic calculus (intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent).
Higher (intellectual) and lower (bodily) pleasures; follow rules that generally maximise happiness; the harm principle.
Ignores justice and rights (tyranny of the majority); consequences are hard to predict; happiness is hard to measure.
Actions are right if they promote happiness and wrong if they produce the reverse.
'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.'
Act judges each situation; rule follows rules that generally produce the greatest happiness.
Simple, democratic, considers consequences and treats each person's happiness equally.
Voluntary, non-voluntary, active and passive euthanasia. Sanctity of life vs quality of life and autonomy.
Natural law opposes it (preserving life); situation ethics may support it if loving; Kant: autonomy vs duty to preserve life; utilitarianism weighs suffering.
Corporate social responsibility, whistleblowing, good ethics as good business, and globalisation.
Kant: never treat employees or customers only as means. Utilitarianism: maximise wellbeing of stakeholders.
Life is sacred and God-given (Genesis 1:27); only God may take it.
Peter Singer: what matters is the quality of life and the person's interests, not life itself.
Examples of countries where forms of euthanasia or assisted dying are legal.
Exposing wrongdoing in a company; Kant may support it as a duty to truth, while it may harm stakeholders.
Moral terms describe natural facts and can be verified, e.g. utilitarianism.
Moore: 'good' is indefinable but recognised by intuition; the naturalistic fallacy and the open question argument.
Ayer: moral statements express emotions ('boo/hurrah' theory) and are neither true nor false.
Synderesis (innate knowledge of good) and conscientia (applying it with reason).
Conscience is the super-ego, formed from parental and social rules, causing guilt.
Debates on premarital and extramarital sex and homosexuality, applying natural law, situation ethics, Kant and utilitarianism.
Cognitivist theories say moral statements can be true or false; non-cognitivist theories say they cannot.
Hare: moral statements are prescriptions that should be universalisable.
Conscience is a God-given faculty of reflection that guides self-love and benevolence.
Authoritarian conscience (internalised authority) vs humanistic conscience (our own true self).
Before the Fall humans lived in harmony; original sin brought concupiscence. Grace is needed for salvation.
Heaven, hell and purgatory; the parable of the sheep and the goats; election debates (limited vs universal salvation).
Natural knowledge (reason and creation, sensus divinitatis - Calvin) vs revealed knowledge (scripture, Jesus Christ).
Son of God, teacher of wisdom and liberator; examples include his miracles, the Sermon on the Mount and challenging authorities.
Theonomous (Bible alone), heteronomous (Bible, church and reason) and autonomous (love) approaches.
Christian duty to resist tyranny; costly vs cheap grace; religionless Christianity; involvement in the plot against Hitler.
Exclusivism, inclusivism (Rahner's anonymous Christians) and pluralism (Hick).
Ruether: God as female; Daly: 'if God is male, then the male is God'.
Freud and Dawkins saw religion as harmful; debates about faith schools and the role of Christianity in public life.
Arose in Latin America; preferential option for the poor; uses Marxist analysis of structural sin (Gutiérrez, Boff).
Concupiscence made sexual desire uncontrolled after the Fall.
God chooses the elect for salvation in advance (double predestination).
A Catholic belief in a state of purification before heaven; rejected by most Protestants.
Different religions are paths to the same Real; the Copernican revolution in theology.
Cheap grace is forgiveness without repentance; costly grace requires following Jesus.
Ruether argued that Jesus challenged patriarchy; the Church has been shaped by male power.
Liberation theology uses Marx's analysis of exploitation but rejects his atheism.
Religion is a delusion that causes harm; faith schools indoctrinate children.
